extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / classical economics
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a classical political-economy textbook (Adam Smith) explaining the nature, division, accumulation, and employment of stock/capital and distinctions used to analyze national revenue. Focuses on definitions, categories, and functional relationships among types of stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of stock for division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: In a rude state without division of labour no stock need be accumulated; once division of labour is introduced, stock must be stored up beforehand to maintain specialists until they complete and sell their produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: a weaver cannot pursue his peculiar business unless a stock exists to maintain him and supply materials/tools until he has completed and sold his web. Accumulation of stock is both prior to and conducive to greater subdivision of labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: stock reserved for immediate consumption vs capital
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's whole stock is distinguished into the part expected to afford revenue (capital) and the part reserved for immediate consumption (food, clothes, furniture, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consumption-reserved stock may be (1) originally set aside, (2) the incoming revenue as it arrives, or (3) previously purchased things not yet consumed. A dwelling-house as a personal dwelling is part of this immediate-consumption stock (does not itself produce public revenue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of employing capital: circulating vs fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital may be employed either (1) in raising/manufacturing/purchasing goods and selling them again (circulating capital) or (2) in improvements, machines, instruments, etc., that yield revenue without changing masters (fixed capital).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchant capital is typically entirely circulating (constant change of form). Fixed capital yields revenue by remaining with its owner (e.g., farm improvements, tools). Each mode yields profit differently and requires different supporting arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals employed in the purchase/production and resale of goods which yield profit only by circulating or changing masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes money in circulation, stocks of provisions, raw materials, and finished work in merchants' hands. The merchant's goods and the money that buys them are paradigmatic circulating capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fixed capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals employed in improvements of land, purchase of useful machines and instruments, and similar items that yield revenue or profit without changing masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed capital examples: machinery, furnaces, buildings used in trade, improved farms, and acquired useful abilities. Fixed capital increases productive power without circulating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational differences in fixed vs circulating capital proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different occupations require different ratios of fixed to circulating capital depending on the nature of the trade's instruments and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a tailor needs little fixed capital (needles), a weaver needs more, an iron-work or mine requires very large fixed capital (furnaces, machinery). The master's circulating capital mainly covers wages and materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold division of a society's general stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The general stock of a country divides naturally into three portions: (1) stock reserved for immediate consumption, (2) fixed capital, and (3) circulating capital, each with distinct functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each portion plays a role in supporting labour, production, and distribution; the text details the composition and roles of each portion and how they interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of fixed capital (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed capital consists chiefly of: (1) useful machines and instruments of trade; (2) profitable buildings (shops, warehouses, farm buildings); (3) improvements of land (clearing, draining, manuring); (4) acquired and useful abilities of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired abilities (education, apprenticeship) are treated as capital fixed in persons. Improved farms are compared to machines in facilitating labour and lasting durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of circulating capital (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulating capital is composed of: (1) money for circulation; (2) stock of provisions in hands of producers/merchants; (3) materials (raw or partially manufactured); (4) finished work held by merchants and manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three of these parts (provisions, materials, finished work) are regularly withdrawn from circulating capital into fixed capital or immediate-consumption stock over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence: fixed capital requires circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fixed capital is both originally derived from and requires continual support by circulating capital; no fixed capital can yield revenue without circulating capital supplying materials and labour maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines and land produce nothing without the circulating capital that provides materials, wages, and maintenance; thus both capitals are functionally interdependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of fixed and circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Both fixed and circulating capitals exist to maintain and augment the stock reserved for immediate consumption, which feeds, clothes, and houses the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The well-being (riches or poverty) of a society depends on how much its capitals can supply to immediate-consumption stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources replenishing circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual supplies for circulating capital come principally from the produce of land, mines, and fisheries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources supply provisions, materials, and money necessary for circulating capital; they replace items withdrawn into fixed capital or immediate consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross revenue vs neat revenue distinction (society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross revenue of a country is the whole annual produce of land and labour; neat revenue is what remains after deducting the expense of maintaining fixed and circulating capital (i.e., what can be freely consumed without encroaching on capital).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to private estate: gross rent vs neat rent; real wealth measured by neat revenue. The expense of maintaining fixed capital must be excluded from neat revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of maintaining fixed capital excluded from neat revenue; circulating maintenance treated differently
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole expense of maintaining fixed capital is excluded from neat revenue because materials and labour used to support fixed capital are diverted from immediate consumption; maintenance of circulating capital, however, often goes into the neat revenue when not used to support fixed capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of circulating capital's four parts, provisions, materials, and finished work are regularly withdrawn and become part of neat revenue unless employed to maintain fixed capital; money's role differs (used to circulate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in fixed capital increase productive power and yield profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper expenditure on fixed capital (repairs, better machinery, improved buildings) increases the productive powers of labour and is repaid with profit, augmenting annual produce more than the support required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: better machinery reduces maintenance expense and enables employment of additional materials and workers; repairs can increase neat rent akin to reduced repair costs on an estate.
